title: The line you'll keep
hookLine: choose one line from this year to carry into the next

cards: Early each morning at the Darbar Sahib in Amritsar, after the Guru Granth Sahib is carried in and opened, a granthi reads out a single hymn. That one hymn becomes the word for the day.
In many gurdwaras it's written on a board near the door. Families send it to each other before breakfast. Someone in London reads the same lines as someone in Ludhiana, and carries them to work.
One hymn, held for one day. Today, one line, held for a year. Hukamnama.

teach.h: HUKAMNAMA: THE DAY'S ORDER FROM THE GRANTH.
teach.b: That morning hymn is called the hukamnama: the order, or the command, of the day. Hukam is a word from the Japji, the divine order that everything moves within; the hukamnama is that order as a page you can read.

teach.h: ONE HYMN, CARRIED THROUGH ONE DAY.
teach.b: The Guru Granth Sahib is opened, not to a favorite place but wherever it opens, and the hymn beginning at the top of the left-hand page is read aloud as the Guru's word for the sangat today.

Sikhs do the same at weddings, namings, and the start of new things. Gurdwaras post it, families text it, people turn it over at red lights. So holding one piece of bani for a stretch of time is an old Sikh habit.

teach.h: A HANDFUL OF LINES FROM THIS YEAR.
teach.b: Here are a few from this year to choose among. Namastvam akaale: salutation to the One beyond time. Hamree karo hath dai rachhaa: give me Your hand and keep me safe.
Anand bhaiaa meree maae: I am in bliss, O my mother. Sukhmani's refrain: the jewel of peace is God's ambrosial Name. The ninth Guru: the wise one frightens no one and fears no one.
Or a line from the Ardas: the good of all.

teach.h: CHOOSE THE LINE THAT ASKS SOMETHING.
teach.b: Choose the line that asks something of you, not just the one that sounds good.
Sikhs often say a line of bani works slowly; you come back to it and it keeps opening. You'll hear it differently in March than in October. One more thing.
These are words Sikhs treat as the living Guru, so many write them out carefully and keep them somewhere clean and respectful.

how: Each morning gurdwaras take a hukamnama, opening the Guru Granth Sahib and reading the hymn at the top of the left-hand page, and many Sikhs carry that hymn, or a single line they love, through the day.

the day's hymn, from where the Granth opens

games.q: dawn at the Darbar Sahib. the Guru Granth Sahib has just been opened. what happens next?
o: the sangat votes on a hymn.
the hymn at the top of the left-hand page is read as the hukamnama.
the granthi reads the Japji from the start.
games.why: the hymn at the top of the left-hand page becomes the day's hukamnama, and it's shared far beyond Amritsar.

practice: Close your eyes and let a few lines from this year pass by slowly, like a scroll, and notice which one your mind stops on; that's probably yours.
Write it out, by hand if you can, in English, in Punjabi, or both, for a place you'll see it, like a notebook cover or a card by your bed. Then sit and let the line repeat, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Hukamnama, the Guru's word read out each day from the Guru Granth Sahib, carried the way one line of bani, chosen from this year, is carried into the next.

orig.note: Punjabi: an order or edict; the Guru's word for the day, read from the Granth.

carryVoice: Your line: one line, kept. A year is long enough for one line. See you tomorrow.
